course: Programming for Everybody (Getting Started with Python)
aiGenerationNote:
Create a 9-minute animated video showing a function as a vending machine. The parameters are the slots where you insert coins (arguments). The machine processes the coins and dispenses a product (output). Show multiple parameters as multiple coin slots. Show default parameters as slots that already have coins in them — you can add your own or use the built-in one. screens.title: Function Parameters and Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how functions receive input and how you supply that input when you call them. Parameters are the placeholders listed in a function's definition; arguments are the actual values you pass at a call site. Understanding this difference is essential because parameters define a function's interface while arguments determine what data the function operates on at runtime. We'll walk through single-parameter examples, multiple parameters and positional ordering, default values that provide sensible fallbacks, and keyword arguments that improve readability. You'll also see how parameters are local to each call, which prevents side effects when you re-use functions with different inputs. A concrete example you will study is a simple greeting function that accepts a name, then a version that takes both name and age. We'll show how Python assigns each evaluated argument to its matching parameter, including when you pass an expression or the result of another function. A common misconception is that parameters are references to the original variables outside the function; for immutable types you get a copy-like behavior and for mutable types behavior differs — we'll explore the immutable case here and point to later lessons for mutable types. By the end you'll be able to design small reusable functions that accept meaningful input and call them safely with positional or keyword arguments.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Parameters are placeholders in a function definition; arguments are the values you pass when calling the function. This distinction shapes how functions accept and use input.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Overview
Function Parameters and Arguments
Learn how functions accept input through parameters and how callers fill those slots with arguments.
In this lesson
You will see parameter definitions, argument usage, default values, and keyword arguments with clear code examples and practical tips.
Why it matters
Functions that accept input are reusable and expressive. Mastering parameters and arguments helps you write clearer APIs and fewer bugs.
Concept Map
Parameters: placeholders; Arguments: provided values; Defaults: fallback values; Keywords: named matching.
Parameter
Argument
Default
Keyword
Explore Key Topics
Three practical focuses you'll study in depth.
Personalization
Use parameters to make one function handle many inputs, like personalized greetings.
Defaults
Give sensible defaults so callers can omit optional information safely.
Keywords
Name important arguments to improve readability and avoid ordering mistakes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the technical difference between a parameter and an argument, define functions that accept one or more parameters, and call functions while passing values both positionally and by name. You will also learn how Python assigns those argument values to the function's internal variables, and how default parameter values work when a caller omits an argument. Each objective ties to a practical skill: reading and writing function signatures, choosing when to use keyword arguments for clarity, and avoiding common mistakes like placing defaults before required parameters. For example, you will write a greet function that takes a name and an optional greeting, and then call it with positional values in one case and with a keyword for the greeting in another. You will practice predicting what values are visible inside a function and why changing a parameter's value inside the function does not change an unrelated outer variable for immutable types. These competencies are fundamental for building clear programs, reusing logic safely, and preparing for more advanced topics like mutable parameters which come later.

screens.title: What you'll practice
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide highlights the hands-on practices you'll use to internalize the concepts. You will implement small functions such as a greeting function, an addition function, and a rectangle inspector that calculates area and perimeter. For each function you'll call it several times with different argument styles: positional values, expressions, and keyword names. You'll also practice setting default values so an argument can be omitted without breaking the call. As you test these functions, observe that each call creates fresh local parameter variables that only exist for that invocation. That means you can safely reuse parameter names across calls without unexpected cross-talk. A useful mental model is to imagine parameters as labeled slots inside a machine that are filled with argument values when the machine runs; once the machine stops, those filled slots vanish. During practice, try intentionally swapping argument order to see how positional arguments match parameters by position and how keyword arguments remove that restriction. These exercises build the intuition that parameters define the function's interface while arguments are the values that vary across calls.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Practice
Hands-on activities
  • Write greet(name) to print a personalized greeting and call it with several names.
  • Write add(a, b) and call with literals and variables to confirm results.
  • Write describe_rectangle(width, height) to compute area and perimeter and test different sizes.

Quick tip
When experimenting, print both inside and outside the function to observe parameter scope and confirm values are local to each call.
Try this
Call the same function twice with different arguments. Notice each call gets its own set of parameter values that do not interfere with each other.

screens.title: Why functions need input
screens.narratorSegment: A function without input always does the same thing and is limited. When we give a function parameters, it can adapt to different data, becoming reusable across many situations. For example, a function that prints the same message every time can't greet different people. By adding a parameter named name, that function can accept any string and say hello to different users. Conceptually, a parameter is a named slot in a function's signature; it does not hold a value until the function is called. An argument is the value that fills that slot at call time. This slot-and-fill model helps you design functions with clear interfaces. A common misunderstanding is to think parameters are global variables that persist beyond the function. They do not. They are local and temporary, existing only while the function runs. Practically, you will often start by thinking about what information a function needs to perform its task, then add parameters for those pieces of information. For instance, a rectangle inspector needs width and height; a greeting needs a name. Asking 'what does this function need?' yields a clean parameter list and clearer code.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Parameters name the inputs a function expects; arguments provide the actual values when calling the function.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Why functions need input
Concept: parameters give flexibility
Identify what a function needs to do its work and declare parameters for those pieces of information.
Parameters are placeholders named in the function definition.
Arguments are the actual values supplied when calling the function.
Ask: what data does this function need? That becomes the parameter list.
Key Takeaway
Parameters let functions operate on different inputs, turning one routine into many useful behaviors.
Analogy
Think of a function as a recipe and parameters as blank ingredient slots. Arguments are the actual ingredients you add when cooking.
Example:
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

greet("Alice")
# Alice is the argument filling the name parameter
Misconception: parameters are not persistent globals; they exist only during the call.

screens.title: Parameters vs. Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: This screen contrasts parameters and arguments to remove confusion. Parameters are part of the function's signature — they name the values a function expects. They are defined by the function author and are local variables created when the function runs. Arguments are the real values given by the caller at runtime. When you call a function Python evaluates every argument expression, then assigns those evaluated values to the matching parameters. A practical example: the definition that names name is where you declare a parameter. When you call the function with the string Alice, that string is the argument. A common mistake is to swap terminology and call the parameter an argument or vice versa, which leads to unclear explanations and misunderstandings when debugging. Another useful distinction is responsibility: the function defines parameters; the caller provides arguments. Remember that parameters are placeholders in the A P I, whereas arguments are usage details. To cement this, try reading a function signature and a call side-by-side and identifying which names are parameters and which values are arguments. Parameters vs. Arguments means parameters define the interface; arguments are the call-time values that fill that interface.. In practical terms, clear language for two different roles. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Parameters vs Arguments
Parameter (definition)
Named in the function signature and acts as a local variable while the function runs.
Example label: name in def greet(name):
Mnemonic: think of a parameter as an empty labeled slot in the function.
Argument (call)
The actual value or expression you pass when invoking a function.
Example label: "Alice" in greet("Alice")
Mnemonic: think of an argument as the ingredient you add to a slot.
Quick practice
def greet(name): # name is parameter
greet("Alice") # "Alice" is argument
Misconception: parameters are not the same as arguments and do not hold values until a call assigns them.

screens.title: Single-parameter example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete code example that uses one parameter. The greeting function declares a parameter named name and uses the print function to assemble a personalized message. When you call the function, you supply a string such as Alice or Bob. Python evaluates the argument expressions and binds the resulting values to the parameter variable inside the function. That parameter behaves like a new, local variable; you can read it and use it in expressions within the function body. A common practical test is to call the same function multiple times with different arguments to see the difference in output. Also try passing a variable instead of a literal to confirm that the function receives the variable's value. In the editor below you'll find the function definition and a few calls; run them mentally or in your editor and verify that the printed lines change according to the argument. Remember: the name parameter exists only during the function execution and is discarded afterward. Try the small experiment of printing the name variable outside the function to see the NameError and understand parameter scope.

keyIdea.title: Walkthrough
keyIdea.text: Define def greet(name): then call greet with different arguments to see how the parameter receives values per call.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Single-parameter example
Code example
def greet(name):
    print(f"Hello, {name}!")

# Calls with different arguments

greet("Alice")
greet("Bob")
Note: the string values Alice and Bob are arguments; name is the parameter created at each call.
Explanation and checks
  • When greet runs, Python sets the local variable name to the passed string.
  • Each call creates a fresh name variable; values from one call do not persist to the next.
  • Try printing name outside the function to observe a NameError and confirm scope rules.
Common mistake
Confusing parameter and argument names when both exist; prefer descriptive parameter names to avoid this.

screens.title: Multiple parameters and positional arguments
screens.narratorSegment: When a function declares more than one parameter, arguments are matched to parameters by position unless you use keywords. The first argument becomes the first parameter, the second argument becomes the second parameter, and so on. This is called positional argument matching. A simple example is a greeting that also prints age: a function with parameters name and age will receive the first passed value into name and the second into age. The order matters: swapping argument order swaps which value goes to which parameter and can produce confusing results. To reduce risk, use clear parameter names and prefer keyword arguments when calling functions that have many parameters or similar value types. Another important practice is to document parameter order in a function's docstring or signature so callers know the intended order. For learners, a quick test is to call the function with different orders or to intentionally swap values to see incorrect outputs — that makes the positional nature concrete and highlights when keywords might be preferable. Multiple parameters and positional arguments means positional arguments are assigned to parameters in order: first-to-first, second-to-second. order therefore matters.. In practical terms, how order determines assignment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Positional matching
keyIdea.text: Positional arguments are assigned to parameters in order: first-to-first, second-to-second. Order therefore matters.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Positional arguments
Example signature
def greet(name, age):
    print(f"Hello, {name}! You are {age} years old.")

# Positional calls
greet("Alice", 25)
greet("Bob", 30)
Order: Alice→name, 25→age. Swapping changes meanings.
Common pitfall
Passing arguments in the wrong order can silently produce incorrect behavior, especially when parameters share the same type.
Mitigation
  • Use keyword arguments for clarity when order is not obvious.
  • Give descriptive parameter names and document the function.
Check your understanding
If you call greet(25, "Alice"), what will name and age contain? Try it to see how position affects values.

screens.title: Parameters are local variables
screens.narratorSegment: Parameters behave like local variables that are created when a function begins and removed when it finishes. This local scope means parameter names are not accessible outside the function body. For example, if a function declares a parameter named text and prints its length, trying to reference text after the function returns causes a name error because the variable no longer exists. This lifetime property prevents accidental interference between different parts of a program: two calls to the same function use independent copies of the parameter variable. A common misconception is to expect that altering a parameter will change the caller's variable; for immutable types like integers and strings, reassignment within the function does not affect the caller because the parameter receives a separate value. This isolation is helpful for reasoning about code: a function can safely rename or manipulate its parameters without worrying about side effects on the caller, unless the argument is a mutable object — which we will study later. Practically, treat parameters as private inputs for the function's internal logic. Parameters are local variables means parameters are local to the function call and cease to exist when the function returns; they do not leak into the outer scope.. In practical terms, scope and lifetime of parameter variables. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scope rule
keyIdea.text: Parameters are local to the function call and cease to exist when the function returns; they do not leak into the outer scope.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Parameter scope
Example: scope error
def show_length(text):
    print(f"Length: {len(text)}")

show_length("Hello")
print(text)  # NameError: text is not defined
The print outside the function fails because text only exists during the function call.
Implication for design
Because parameters are local, functions should return values when callers need results instead of depending on parameter names to persist.
Analogy: each call gets its own workspace; when the work finishes the workspace is cleared.
Key Takeaway

Parameters create temporary, local variables. They help keep functions self-contained and reduce accidental interactions.

screens.title: Arguments can be expressions
screens.narratorSegment: You are not limited to passing literal values as arguments. Arguments can be variables, arithmetic expressions, or the return value from another function. When a call is made, Python evaluates each argument expression first, then assigns the resulting value to the corresponding parameter. For instance, if you pass the variable n or the expression 3 plus 4 to a function that doubles its input, the function receives the evaluated numbers two and seven respectively. This flexibility makes code concise because you can compute values inline and pass them directly. A practical exercise: write a function that doubles a value and call it with a variable, then with an expression adding two numbers, and finally with the result of a length operation on a string. A common misconception is to assume that passing an expression will delay its evaluation until inside the function. In fact, evaluation happens before the call. Remember this evaluation order when writing functions that rely on side effects or when debugging unexpected values. Arguments can be expressions means python evaluates argument expressions first and then assigns their values to parameters when calling a function.. In practical terms, passing variables, calculations, and other function results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Argument evaluation
keyIdea.text: Python evaluates argument expressions first and then assigns their values to parameters when calling a function.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Argument expressions
Examples to try
def double(x):
    print(x * 2)

n = 5
double(n)        # passes value of n
double(3 + 4)    # passes result of arithmetic
double(len("hi"))  # passes result of another function
Each argument expression is evaluated before the function receives its value.
Why this matters
  • It allows concise calls using calculations and other function results.
  • Understanding evaluation order helps avoid surprising side effects or stale values.
  • Use temporary variables if you need to reuse an evaluated result for clarity.
Check your understanding
Predict what a function will print when called with expressions vs variables — then test it to validate your reasoning.

screens.title: Value copying for simple types
screens.narratorSegment: With simple immutable types like integers and strings, parameters receive a copy-like value so that reassigning the parameter inside the function does not affect the caller's variable. Consider a function that increments its parameter and prints the result. When you pass a numeric variable a into the function, the function's parameter receives the number's value. The function may increase its local parameter variable, but the original variable outside remains unchanged. This demonstrates an important safety property: operations that rebind a parameter name inside a function won't overwrite variables in the caller. This is why the increment example shows that inside the function x becomes one larger, while the outer variable stays at its original value. A common misconception is to think Python uses pass-by-reference for all types; instead, think in terms of values being assigned to parameter names and then mutated or rebound depending on type. We'll explore how mutable types differ in a later lesson, but for now, assume integers and strings behave as value-like copies in this context. Value copying for simple types means for integers and strings, parameter reassignment inside a function does not change the caller's variable; each call gets its own value.. In practical terms, why changing a parameter doesn't change the caller's variable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

def increment(x):

    print(f"Inside function: x = {x}")

a = 5
increment(a)
print(f"Outside function: a = {a}")
# Inside: x is 6

Reassigning x inside the function does not change a outside the function for immutable types.

screens.title: Default parameter values
screens.narratorSegment: Default parameter values let you make arguments optional by specifying a fallback in the function definition. If a caller omits that argument, Python uses the default you provided. A clear example is a greeting that accepts name and an optional greeting word, where greeting defaults to Hello. Calling the function with only a name uses the default greeting; supplying a greeting overrides it. Defaults are useful to reduce repetition and to provide sensible behavior while still allowing customization. A critical rule is that parameters with default values must come after parameters without defaults; placing a default before a required parameter is a syntax error. When designing APIs, choose defaults carefully so they represent common or safe behavior. A common pitfall is using a mutable object as a default — that has subtle shared-state consequences, so for now prefer immutable defaults like strings or numbers. Using defaults improves ergonomics: callers can use simple calls in the common case and override only when needed. Default parameter values means default values provide optional parameters; they are used when the caller omits the corresponding argument.. In practical terms, provide fallbacks so arguments can be optional. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Default parameter ordering rules
screens.narratorSegment: Python requires that parameters with default values come after parameters without defaults. The reason is simple: positional matching would be ambiguous if a required parameter followed a defaulted one. If you write a function signature that places a defaulted parameter first and a required parameter second, Python raises a syntax error. This rule enforces clarity in the function interface and keeps positional calls predictable. When designing functions, put required parameters first, then optional ones with reasonable defaults. If you need a required argument after optional ones for some reason, prefer keyword arguments at call sites to maintain clarity. A concrete failure case to try is to declare a function with a default before a required parameter and watch the interpreter report the syntax error; it helps reinforce the rule. In practice, ordering parameters by required-to-optional is also user-friendly and mirrors common A P I design patterns. Default parameter ordering rules means always place non-default parameters before parameters that have default values to avoid syntax errors and ambiguity.. screens.title: Keyword arguments
screens.narratorSegment: Keyword arguments let you pass values by explicitly naming the parameter at the call site. This removes the dependence on argument order and improves readability when functions have many parameters. For example, a function describe_pet with parameters animal, name, and age can be called with animal equals dog, name equals Rex, age equals three in any order when you use keywords. This makes code self-documenting because the caller's intent is visible in the call. A common misconception is that keywords are slower or less idiomatic — they are perfectly normal and often preferred for clarity. Note that when mixing positional and keyword arguments, positional arguments must come first, followed by keywords. Use keywords intentionally to avoid positional errors and to make your code easier for others to read and maintain. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Let's summarize three essential ideas. First, a parameter is a variable named in a function definition that acts as a placeholder for the value the function will receive. Second, an argument is the actual value you pass when calling a function; Python evaluates each argument expression first and then assigns those values to the corresponding parameters. Third, positional arguments are matched by position — first to first, second to second — so order matters unless you use keyword arguments. These core concepts help you read function signatures and calls correctly. As you code, label parameters clearly, prefer keywords for complex calls, and rely on defaults to make optional information easier to supply. Practically, use small experiments to validate your mental model: print parameter values inside the function, try expressions as arguments, and switch to keyword calls to fix ordering mistakes. These habits will reduce confusion and make your functions clearer and more reusable.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how functions receive input and how you supply that input when you call them. Parameters are the placeholders listed in a function's definition; arguments are the actual values you pass at a call site. Understanding this difference is essential because parameters define a function's interface while arguments determine what data the function operates on at runtime. We'll walk through single-parameter examples, multiple parameters and positional ordering, default values that provide sensible fallbacks, and keyword arguments that improve readability. You'll also see how parameters are local to each call, which prevents side effects when you re-use functions with different inputs. A concrete example you will study is a simple greeting function that accepts a name, then a version that takes both name and age. We'll show how Python assigns each evaluated argument to its matching parameter, including when you pass an expression or the result of another function. A common misconception is that parameters are references to the original variables outside the function; for immutable types you get a copy-like behavior and for mutable types behavior differs — we'll explore the immutable case here and point to later lessons for mutable types. By the end you'll be able to design small reusable functions that accept meaningful input and call them safely with positional or keyword arguments.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain the technical difference between a parameter and an argument, define functions that accept one or more parameters, and call functions while passing values both positionally and by name. You will also learn how Python assigns those argument values to the function's internal variables, and how default parameter values work when a caller omits an argument. Each objective ties to a practical skill: reading and writing function signatures, choosing when to use keyword arguments for clarity, and avoiding common mistakes like placing defaults before required parameters. For example, you will write a greet function that takes a name and an optional greeting, and then call it with positional values in one case and with a keyword for the greeting in another. You will practice predicting what values are visible inside a function and why changing a parameter's value inside the function does not change an unrelated outer variable for immutable types. These competencies are fundamental for building clear programs, reusing logic safely, and preparing for more advanced topics like mutable parameters which come later.

This second objectives slide highlights the hands-on practices you'll use to internalize the concepts. You will implement small functions such as a greeting function, an addition function, and a rectangle inspector that calculates area and perimeter. For each function you'll call it several times with different argument styles: positional values, expressions, and keyword names. You'll also practice setting default values so an argument can be omitted without breaking the call. As you test these functions, observe that each call creates fresh local parameter variables that only exist for that invocation. That means you can safely reuse parameter names across calls without unexpected cross-talk. A useful mental model is to imagine parameters as labeled slots inside a machine that are filled with argument values when the machine runs; once the machine stops, those filled slots vanish. During practice, try intentionally swapping argument order to see how positional arguments match parameters by position and how keyword arguments remove that restriction. These exercises build the intuition that parameters define the function's interface while arguments are the values that vary across calls.

A function without input always does the same thing and is limited. When we give a function parameters, it can adapt to different data, becoming reusable across many situations. For example, a function that prints the same message every time can't greet different people. By adding a parameter named name, that function can accept any string and say hello to different users. Conceptually, a parameter is a named slot in a function's signature; it does not hold a value until the function is called. An argument is the value that fills that slot at call time. This slot-and-fill model helps you design functions with clear interfaces. A common misunderstanding is to think parameters are global variables that persist beyond the function. They do not. They are local and temporary, existing only while the function runs. Practically, you will often start by thinking about what information a function needs to perform its task, then add parameters for those pieces of information. For instance, a rectangle inspector needs width and height; a greeting needs a name. Asking 'what does this function need?' yields a clean parameter list and clearer code.

This screen contrasts parameters and arguments to remove confusion. Parameters are part of the function's signature — they name the values a function expects. They are defined by the function author and are local variables created when the function runs. Arguments are the real values given by the caller at runtime. When you call a function Python evaluates every argument expression, then assigns those evaluated values to the matching parameters. A practical example: the definition that names name is where you declare a parameter. When you call the function with the string Alice, that string is the argument. A common mistake is to swap terminology and call the parameter an argument or vice versa, which leads to unclear explanations and misunderstandings when debugging. Another useful distinction is responsibility: the function defines parameters; the caller provides arguments. Remember that parameters are placeholders in the A P I, whereas arguments are usage details. To cement this, try reading a function signature and a call side-by-side and identifying which names are parameters and which values are arguments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Keyword arguments let you pass values by explicitly naming the parameter at the call site. This removes the dependence on argument order and improves readability when functions have many parameters. For example, a function describe_pet with parameters animal, name, and age can be called with animal equals dog, name equals Rex, age equals three in any order when you use keywords. This makes code self-documenting because the caller's intent is visible in the call. Keyword arguments are especially helpful for optional parameters with defaults or for values whose order is unclear. A common misconception is that keywords are slower or less idiomatic — they are perfectly normal and often preferred for clarity. Note that when mixing positional and keyword arguments, positional arguments must come first, followed by keywords. Use keywords intentionally to avoid positional errors and to make your code easier for others to read and maintain. Let's summarize three essential ideas. First, a parameter is a variable named in a function definition that acts as a placeholder for the value the function will receive. Second, an argument is the actual value you pass when calling a function; Python evaluates each argument expression first and then assigns those values to the corresponding parameters. Third, positional arguments are matched by position — first to first, second to second — so order matters unless you use keyword arguments. These core concepts help you read function signatures and calls correctly. As you code, label parameters clearly, prefer keywords for complex calls, and rely on defaults to make optional information easier to supply. Practically, use small experiments to validate your mental model: print parameter values inside the function, try expressions as arguments, and switch to keyword calls to fix ordering mistakes. These habits will reduce confusion and make your functions clearer and more reusable.

A few practical rules will keep your functions reliable. First, remember that parameters are local: they are created when a function starts and discarded when it ends. Second, default parameter values provide optional behavior, but defaults must appear after required parameters to avoid syntax errors. Third, passing expressions, variables, or other function results as arguments is common — Python evaluates them before assigning to parameters. Watch out for the common pitfall of swapping argument order when using positional calls; consider keywords in those cases. Another frequent source of confusion is assuming parameter reassignment mutates the caller's variable; for immutable types, that does not happen. These concise reminders form the day-to-day checklist when reading or writing functions: check parameter ordering, choose defaults carefully, prefer keywords for clarity, and test by printing parameter values inside functions to validate your understanding.
